bands.label: Manual and fragile
bands.interpretation: Delivery depends heavily on individuals and manual intervention.

bands.label: Emerging
bands.interpretation: Some DevOps practices exist, but major delivery and operations gaps remain.

bands.label: Developing
bands.interpretation: Core practices are present but inconsistent across applications or teams.

bands.label: Mature
bands.interpretation: Delivery is largely repeatable and measurable, with targeted gaps.

bands.label: Optimised
bands.interpretation: Strong delivery and operational practices; the work now is platform scale and continuous improvement.

prerequisite_gates.rationale: A platform built on manual delivery industrialises the manual delivery.

sections.title: Delivery context and release profile
sections.focus: What you ship, and how often
sections.body: Only the release-frequency question here is scored. The other two decide how everything after them should be read — a two-person startup and a fifty-engineer fintech can post the same score and need opposite first moves.

sections.title: Source control and collaboration
sections.focus: Whether a change can be traced
sections.body: This is the cheapest maturity in the whole assessment and the one most often skipped. If you cannot say which commit caused an outage, who reviewed it, and when it shipped, every incident becomes an investigation before it can become a fix.

sections.title: CI/CD and release automation
sections.focus: Build, test, deploy, and roll back
sections.body: The heart of it. Manual deployment is not just slow — it is the reason releases get batched, and batched releases are the reason they are risky. A rollback you have never tested is a plan, not a capability.

sections.title: Infrastructure as Code and environments
sections.body: Infrastructure nobody can rebuild from code is infrastructure nobody can safely change. Environment drift is the quiet version of the same problem: it works in staging, and staging has not looked like production for a year.

sections.title: Testing and security in delivery
sections.focus: What can stop a bad release
sections.body: Checks that report but never block are decoration. This section asks whether quality and security are part of the pipeline or a conversation that happens after it — and, when something is found, whether anyone owns fixing it.

sections.title: Observability and incident response
sections.body: Two questions about whether you can see your systems, and one about what happens when they break. Learning about your outage from a customer is a measurable position, and it is the one this section is looking for.

sections.title: Reliability and operational readiness
sections.body: Delivery gets the attention; operating the thing afterwards is where the cost lands. An untested backup is the clearest example in this whole assessment of something that looks like safety and is not.

sections.title: Team capability and continuous improvement
sections.body: This section predicts the future rather than describing the present. Everything before it can be fixed in one engagement. Only this decides whether it is still fixed in a year.

delivery_automation.title: Delivery automation
delivery_automation.body: Your highest-priority opportunity is delivery automation. Builds, deployments, approvals, or rollbacks still depend on a person doing them correctly under pressure. Start by standardising the whole path — build, test, deploy, approve, roll back — for one representative application, then copy it.
actions: Pick one application and write down every manual step between a merged change and it running in production.
Automate the deployment for that one application end to end, including the rollback.
Test the rollback deliberately, on a normal working day, before you need it.

ci_cd_foundation.title: CI/CD foundation
ci_cd_foundation.body: Establish a CI/CD foundation: version-controlled pipeline configuration, automated validation on every change, promotion between environments, deployment approvals, and a defined rollback. Without this, every other improvement has nowhere to run.
actions: Add a pipeline that builds and tests every pull request, and keep its configuration in the repository.
Make the pipeline the only route to production for one application, then widen it.
Add environment promotion so the artefact tested in staging is the artefact deployed to production.

infrastructure_reproducibility.title: Infrastructure reproducibility
infrastructure_reproducibility.body: Introduce Infrastructure as Code and reusable environment templates, so infrastructure changes are reviewable, repeatable, and recoverable. The test is simple: could you rebuild production from code, and would the result match?
actions: Put one environment under Infrastructure as Code, starting with whatever is easiest to recreate.
Define staging and production from the same templates, with the differences stated as parameters.
Move configuration and secrets into a managed secret service, out of deployment files and chat.

testing_devsecops.title: Testing and DevSecOps
testing_devsecops.body: Move automated tests and security checks earlier in delivery, then define release gates appropriate to each application. A check that reports but cannot block a release is documentation, not a control.
actions: Agree which checks are allowed to block a release, and make those blocking.
Add automated dependency and container scanning to the pipeline rather than to a quarterly review.
Name an owner, a severity scale, and a deadline for security findings before you need them.

observability_gap.title: Observability
observability_gap.body: Build an observability baseline: service health, logs, metrics, traces, alerts that are worth waking someone for, and a named owner for each critical service. If customers report problems before your systems do, this is the first thing to fix.
actions: Centralise logs and metrics for the two or three services that matter most.
Build one dashboard per critical service that answers "is this healthy right now".
Delete or fix every alert nobody acts on, so the remaining ones mean something.

incident_and_reliability.title: Reliability and incident response
incident_and_reliability.body: Establish incident-response ownership, availability targets, recovery runbooks, verified backups, and a review after each incident. Most of this is agreement and writing rather than engineering, which is why it is so often missing.
actions: Define who leads an incident, who communicates, and how it escalates — before the next one.
Restore a backup into a scratch environment and time it. An untested backup is not a backup.
Write a short runbook for the two failures you have already seen more than once.

source_control_traceability.title: Source control and traceability
source_control_traceability.body: Tighten version control and the trail that connects a production change to its commit, reviewer, ticket, and deployment. This is the cheapest maturity available to you and it makes every incident shorter.
actions: Protect the main branch and require review before merge.
Get every piece of code that reaches production into version control, including the scripts.
Link deployments to commits so a production change can be traced without an investigation.

platform_and_capability.title: Platform and team capability
platform_and_capability.body: Define a platform-engineering roadmap — golden paths, reusable templates, developer self-service, standard guardrails — and make delivery performance something you measure rather than debate. Where ownership rests on one or two people, this is also the fix for that.
actions: Write down who owns build, deployment, infrastructure, security, and operations. Fill the gaps that appear.
Turn whatever your best team does into a template the others can start from.
Track deployment frequency, lead time, change-failure rate, and recovery time, and review them monthly.

continuous_improvement.title: Continuous improvement
continuous_improvement.body: No single area stands out as your bottleneck, which at this level is the finding. The work now is holding what you have and improving it deliberately — platform scale, developer experience, and the delivery metrics that show whether either is moving.
actions: Review your delivery metrics on a schedule, and act on the trend rather than the last incident.
Invest in developer self-service so improvement does not depend on a central team.
Re-run this assessment in six months and compare, rather than trusting the impression.

managed_devops.title: A managed DevOps engagement
managed_devops.body: Based on your answers, a managed DevOps engagement is likely to be the fastest route: we establish the foundations, operate the delivery platform with you, and transfer the capability to your team rather than keeping it.
